title: How do you cut per-request overhead at the gateway — connection pooling / HTTP/2 multiplexing to reuse upstream connections instead of a new TCP+TLS handshake each time (target >99% connection reuse), hybrid rate limiting (a local token bucket synced to Redis every ~100ms instead of a Redis round trip per request), async batched logging off the request path, and request coalescing (de-duplicate identical in-flight requests)?
shortTitle: How to cut per-request overhead at the gateway

s1_definition.profdef: Cutting per-request overhead means eliminating the repeated, wasteful work the gateway does for each request so that each request becomes as cheap as possible. The main techniques are: reuse upstream connections through connection pooling and HTTP/2 multiplexing so you avoid a fresh TCP and TLS handshake on every call, aiming for over ninety-nine percent connection reuse; use hybrid rate limiting where a local in-memory token bucket is periodically synced with Redis instead of doing a Redis round trip per request; move logging off the request path by batching it asynchronously; and coalesce identical in-flight requests so duplicate concurrent requests share a single downstream call. Each technique removes a fixed cost that would otherwise be multiplied by total traffic.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India dispatch desk sending documents to the central vault for every customer. If a courier sets up a brand-new secure route to the vault for each document, that setup is wasteful; instead the courier keeps a few secure routes open and reuses them, that is connection reuse. If the clerk phones head office to check each customer's daily limit, that is slow; instead he keeps a local tally and syncs with head office every few seconds, that is hybrid rate limiting. If he stops to file paperwork after every customer, the line jams; instead he drops notes in a tray that someone files in batches, that is async logging. And if three customers ask the exact same question at once, he answers it once and tells all three, that is request coalescing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Make every request cheap by reusing upstream connections, rate limiting locally with periodic Redis sync, batching logs asynchronously off the path, and coalescing identical in-flight requests into one downstream call.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Cutting per-request overhead means eliminating the repeated, wasteful work the gateway does for each request so that each request becomes as cheap as possible. The main techniques are: reuse upstream connections through connection pooling and HTTP/2 multiplexing so you avoid a fresh TCP and TLS handshake on every call, aiming for over ninety-nine percent connection reuse; use hybrid rate limiting where a local in-memory token bucket is periodically synced with Redis instead of doing a Redis round trip per request; move logging off the request path by batching it asynchronously; and coalesce identical in-flight requests so duplicate concurrent requests share a single downstream call. Each technique removes a fixed cost that would otherwise be multiplied by total traffic.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India dispatch desk sending documents to the central vault for every customer. If a courier sets up a brand-new secure route to the vault for each document, that setup is wasteful; instead the courier keeps a few secure routes open and reuses them, that is connection reuse. If the clerk phones head office to check each customer's daily limit, that is slow; instead he keeps a local tally and syncs with head office every few seconds, that is hybrid rate limiting. If he stops to file paperwork after every customer, the line jams; instead he drops notes in a tray that someone files in batches, that is async logging. And if three customers ask the exact same question at once, he answers it once and tells all three, that is request coalescing.

**One line to remember:** Make every request cheap by reusing upstream connections, rate limiting locally with periodic Redis sync, batching logs asynchronously off the path, and coalescing identical in-flight requests into one downstream call.

sections.s2_technical:
The first and often biggest overhead is connection setup. Opening a new connection to an upstream service means a TCP handshake and, for TLS, a cryptographic TLS handshake, which together cost several network round trips and real CPU. If the gateway opens a fresh connection per request, this handshake cost is paid over and over. The fix is a connection pool that keeps established connections open and reuses them across requests, so the handshake is amortized. HTTP/2 goes further with multiplexing, letting many concurrent requests share a single connection, which dramatically reduces the number of connections needed. The practical target is over ninety-nine percent connection reuse, meaning fewer than one in a hundred requests pays for a new handshake. In a reactive gateway you configure the HTTP client's pool size and keep-alive so connections are reused aggressively.

The second overhead is rate limiting that touches a shared store per request. A naive distributed rate limiter does a Redis round trip for every request to check and update the counter, which adds network latency to every single request and makes Redis a hot dependency. The hybrid approach keeps a local token bucket in the gateway's memory, which it checks instantly with no network, and periodically, say every hundred milliseconds, syncs the local counts with Redis to stay approximately consistent across replicas. This trades a small amount of precision, because the global count is slightly stale between syncs, for a huge reduction in per-request latency and Redis load. For most rate-limiting purposes, approximate global limits are perfectly acceptable.

The third overhead is logging and other bookkeeping done synchronously on the request path. Writing a log line to disk or shipping it over the network inline makes the request wait for I/O. The fix is to enqueue log events into an in-memory buffer that a background worker flushes in batches, so the request only pays a near-instant enqueue and the actual write happens off the hot path. The same idea applies to metrics and audit events. The one caution is that a crash could lose buffered events, so for critical audit data you choose the durability trade-off deliberately.

The fourth overhead appears under bursty load: many identical requests in flight at the same time. If a hundred clients ask for the same cacheable resource simultaneously and it is not yet cached, a naive gateway makes a hundred identical downstream calls, which is both wasteful and can stampede the backend. Request coalescing, also called request collapsing or single-flight, detects that an identical request is already in flight and makes the duplicates wait for and share that one result instead of launching their own calls. So a hundred simultaneous identical requests become one downstream call whose single response is returned to all hundred.

A senior nuance is that these optimizations interact and must be measured. Connection pooling needs tuning so the pool is neither too small, causing contention, nor too large, exhausting upstream capacity. Hybrid rate limiting needs a sync interval balanced against how strict the limit must be. Coalescing only applies safely to idempotent, identical requests, never to distinct money-moving operations. Another nuance is that the goal is always the same: remove any fixed per-request cost, because at the edge that cost is multiplied by the entire system's throughput, so shaving microseconds per request yields enormous aggregate savings.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's gateway opened a new TLS connection to the account service for every request, did a Redis round trip to check the rate limit for every request, and logged synchronously. Under salary-week load, the handshake cost and the Redis round trips dominated latency, and a burst of identical balance lookups for a popular shared account caused a stampede of duplicate downstream calls.

Problem 2 — Each of these costs individually looked small, but multiplied by the traffic they became the dominant overhead, so we needed to cut them all.

The connection to the fix: we will model each optimization. A connection pool reuses upstream connections and reports the reuse rate. A hybrid rate limiter checks a local bucket and only periodically syncs to a simulated Redis. An async logger batches off the path. A request coalescer collapses identical in-flight lookups into one call. The demo contrasts the naive per-request costs with the optimized ones and reports the savings.

What the code will do. There is a `ConnectionPool` tracking new handshakes versus reuses. There is a `HybridRateLimiter` with a local bucket and a periodic sync counter. There is an `AsyncBatchLogger`. There is a `RequestCoalescer` using single-flight. There is an `OptimizedGateway` wiring them together. The demo runs many requests, including a burst of identical lookups, and reports connection reuse percentage, Redis sync count versus request count, and coalesced call savings.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is two hundred steady requests followed by a burst of fifty identical concurrent lookups for one hot account.

Step 1. For the steady requests, each one first checks the hybrid rate limiter. The limiter checks the local in-memory bucket instantly, with no network, and only syncs to Redis when the hundred-millisecond interval has elapsed. So across two hundred fast requests there are only a handful of Redis syncs instead of two hundred Redis round trips.

Step 2. Each steady request then acquires an upstream connection from the pool. The first few requests cause new handshakes to grow the pool, but after that the pool reuses existing connections, so the overwhelming majority of requests pay no handshake cost. The reported reuse percentage climbs well above ninety-nine percent as traffic continues.

Step 3. Each steady request also logs, but it only enqueues the log line into the async batch logger, which returns almost instantly. The actual writing happens in the background in batches of fifty, entirely off the request path, so the request never waits for I/O.

Step 4. For the burst, fifty threads simultaneously look up the same hot account. The coalescer sees the first thread launch a single downstream call and registers it as in-flight. The other forty-nine threads find that identical request already in flight and simply wait for and share its result, rather than each making their own call. So fifty identical concurrent lookups collapse into essentially one downstream call.

Step 5. The report ties it together: connection reuse is well above ninety-nine percent, Redis was synced only a few times instead of per request, logging never blocked the path, and the fifty-request burst produced only a tiny number of real downstream calls thanks to coalescing. Each technique removed a fixed per-request cost, and because those costs were multiplied by all the traffic, the aggregate savings are large.

```
2026-10-24 15:00:01 [INFO] === Steady traffic: connection reuse + hybrid rate limit + async log ===
2026-10-24 15:00:01 [INFO] === Burst: 50 identical in-flight lookups → coalesced to 1 call ===
2026-10-24 15:00:01 [INFO] Connection reuse = 99.5% (new handshakes=1)
2026-10-24 15:00:01 [INFO] Redis syncs=2 (vs per-request Redis calls avoided)
2026-10-24 15:00:01 [INFO] Coalescing: downstreamCalls=2 coalesced=48 (50 identical → few real calls)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Cutting per-request overhead means eliminating the repeated, wasteful work the gateway does for each request, because at the edge every fixed cost is multiplied by the entire system's throughput, so shaving even microseconds per request yields enormous aggregate savings. I focus on four techniques. The first is connection reuse. Opening a new connection to an upstream service means a TCP handshake and a TLS handshake, which cost several round trips and real CPU, so I use a connection pool with keep-alive and HTTP/2 multiplexing to reuse established connections across many requests. The target I aim for is over ninety-nine percent connection reuse, meaning fewer than one in a hundred requests pays for a fresh handshake. In my banking work at National Bank of India, this alone removed a large chunk of latency during salary-week spikes.

The second is hybrid rate limiting. A naive distributed limiter does a Redis round trip on every request to check and update the counter, which adds network latency to every request and makes Redis a hot dependency. Instead I keep a local token bucket in the gateway's memory, which I check instantly with no network, and I sync the local counts with Redis only periodically, roughly every hundred milliseconds. This trades a little precision, because the global count is slightly stale between syncs, for a huge drop in per-request latency and Redis load, and for rate limiting an approximate global limit is almost always acceptable.

The third is moving logging off the request path. Writing logs synchronously makes the request wait for disk or network I/O, so instead I enqueue log events into an in-memory buffer that a background worker flushes in batches, and the request only pays a near-instant enqueue. The one trade-off I am honest about is that a crash could lose buffered events, so for critical audit data I choose the durability trade-off deliberately. The fourth is request coalescing, also called single-flight, for bursty load. If fifty clients ask for the same not-yet-cached resource at the same time, a naive gateway makes fifty identical downstream calls and can stampede the backend; with coalescing, the first request launches one downstream call and the other forty-nine wait for and share that single result, so fifty simultaneous identical requests become essentially one call.

The nuances I always add are that these must be tuned and measured, and applied safely. The connection pool size must be balanced so it is neither too small, causing contention, nor too large, exhausting upstream capacity. The rate-limiter sync interval balances latency against how strict the limit must be. And coalescing is only ever applied to idempotent, identical reads, never to distinct money-moving operations, because collapsing two different transfers would be a correctness disaster. The unifying principle is simple: remove any fixed per-request cost, because at the edge that cost is paid by the whole system.
